title: Shopify AI Search: How to Make Your Products Easier for AI Shopping Tools to Understand
excerpt: Buyers increasingly ask in plain language. This is the part of AI product discovery a merchant actually controls: accurate titles, complete attributes, honest availability, and a discovery audit you can run on a sample of the catalogue.
intro: A customer asks for a lightweight travel stroller that folds small enough for a city car. If your store sells exactly that product, whether it gets matched comes down to the title, the attributes, and the variant data — not to anything you can configure for an AI system specifically. Nobody can promise that a shopping assistant will recommend a given product. What a store can do is make sure the data the system reads is actually right, and this guide covers that part: the product record itself, and how to audit it.

sections.heading: What AI shopping search means for Shopify stores
paragraphs: For a decade, product discovery worked one way: a crawler reads pages, a person types keywords, a ranked list sits in between. That loop is not going anywhere, but it is no longer the only path a product gets found by. Shopping assistants and *agentic storefronts* read structured product information — title, options, price, availability — and match it against a request made in *plain language*.

This is documented platform direction rather than speculation. Shopify describes [Shopify Catalog](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-shopify-catalog) and [agentic storefront product discovery](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-sales-channels/agentic-storefronts/products) in its own documentation. The practical split follows from that: a merchant controls the input — the accuracy, completeness, and consistency of the product data. Each downstream system decides for itself what to do with it, and that decision is not published, configurable, or guaranteed.

So the work is not new. It is the same work a careful store should be doing anyway — cleaning product data, completing attributes, keeping variants and stock honest — now with more readers of the record than a crawler.

sections.heading: How product discovery differs from traditional keyword search
paragraphs: Keyword search matches text. A customer types “travel stroller” and gets pages that contain those words, which is why so many stores stuff synonyms into titles and meta descriptions: the store's job was to make sure the right words were on the right pages.

A natural-language request does not work that way. “Folds small for a city car” contains no keyword a title will ever contain. A system answering it has to reason over *structured attributes* — folded dimensions, weight, intended use. The closer the data is to a machine-readable record of what the product actually is, the more reliably it matches, whether the reader is a search engine, a filter, a comparison, or an agent.
The same cleanup helps ordinary customers, because the person narrowing a collection by size and colour is doing a smaller version of the same task.

sections.heading: Which product attributes help shoppers and systems understand a product
paragraphs: Start with the title, the first field every reader meets. A useful title names the product, its category, and one or two genuinely distinguishing facts. “Babymore Travel System, 3-in-1, with car seat” can be matched against a request. “The Ultimate Premium Bundle!” cannot, because it states nothing that is checkable.

Then the attributes: materials, dimensions, weight, size, compatibility. A travel system that lists its folded dimensions in centimetres and kilograms can be matched to the question “will this fit in a hatchback trunk.” A listing that says “compact and convenient” cannot. *Folded dimensions* are the difference between a record a system can use and marketing copy it has to ignore.

Then the variants. Each purchasable combination is its own record with its own price, stock state, and image. A variant that is sold out but not marked as such corrupts every system that reads the record, and it is visible to customers on a documented storefront like the one in the [product record note from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-product-data) — where the record has to survive the trip from admin to checkout. Availability matters in the same way: a system that recommends a product that is actually unavailable has failed the shopper twice, once with a wrong match and once with a dead end.

sections.heading: How to review product data in Shopify
paragraphs: The review happens in three places. First, the product editor in the admin: open ten products at random and check each field against the physical product. Where the product is 6.4 kg, the record should say 6.4 kg, not “lightweight.”

Second, the product page itself. Titles and descriptions are sometimes transformed by the theme; price and availability render from live data; images come from the media library. What you are verifying is *the rendered record* — title, specifications, variants, price, availability — on the page a buyer actually reads. The desktop detail view is the honest test, and it is what the featured image on this article shows.

Third, the structured output the page ships. Product pages emit a machine-readable summary of name, price, currency, and availability, and if that summary disagrees with the rendered page, the page has two conflicting records. That problem gets its own guide: [Shopify Product Schema: Fix Structured Data Errors](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors).

A rhythm that keeps it from rotting: review a random sample weekly, every product you touch monthly, the full catalogue quarterly. Catalogue quality is maintenance, the same way [store maintenance](/shopify-store-maintenance) is — not a one-time migration project.

sections.heading: Shopify Catalog, AI channels, and what merchants can control
paragraphs: Shopify is building the infrastructure for products to be discovered through channels a merchant does not operate directly — agentic storefronts, shopping assistants, other AI-mediated surfaces. [Shopify's documentation on agentic storefront products](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-sales-channels/agentic-storefronts/products) is the primary reference for how product discovery is intended to work there, and [the Shopify Catalog write-up](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-shopify-catalog) covers the catalog layer underneath.
The boundary is worth stating plainly: there is no per-product toggle, no guaranteed placement, no published ranking for these surfaces. The input is the data. The output is each system's decision.

I treat emerging channels the way I treat any channel I do not operate: prepare the record, publish it cleanly, and do not buy certainty that does not exist. If the data is accurate enough to serve a customer, it is accurate enough to be understood — that is the part worth engineering for.

For stores that need this done at catalogue scale — attributes backfilled, variants normalized, schema verified across thousands of products — it is development work. It is the kind of [Shopify development](/shopify-development) I take on, and it is the kind of work that gets written up in the [Commerce Journal](/blogs) when there is something specific to report.

sections.heading: A practical product-discovery audit
paragraphs: Pick a representative sample — twenty products spanning your best sellers, your newest arrivals, and the long tail — and score each one against a fixed list:

Title: does it name the product, its category, and at least one distinguishing fact, without filler? Attributes: are materials, dimensions, weight, size, and compatibility present where the product has them? Variants: does every purchasable combination exist as a real variant with its own price and stock state? Availability: do in-stock, low-stock, and sold-out states render correctly on the page? Descriptions: do they add anything the title does not? Structured data: does the page's product markup match the rendered price, currency, and availability?

Write the findings as *patterns, not line items*. “Folded dimensions missing on most travel systems” is an action; “product 2317 is incomplete” is noise. The patterns become the backfill plan, which is the workflow the [product data management guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) covers — turning ad-hoc cleanup into a repeatable catalogue process.
When the audit shows attributes missing at scale, the fix is not twenty manual edits. It is a standardized attribute set, a bulk update, and a validation pass.

sections.heading: Mistakes to avoid — and what AI visibility cannot guarantee
paragraphs: Stuffing titles with keywords in hopes of matching a machine. The systems that reason over product data reward completeness and accuracy, not density; a title optimized for a search engine in 2015 is harder to match in 2026.

Treating “AI visibility” as a deliverable. I will not promise that a given change makes an assistant recommend a given product, because no one can. What a clean record does remove is a class of mismatches — the wrong attribute, the wrong price, the phantom stock — that any reader of your data would hit.

Optimizing the record but not the storefront. If filters do not work, a shopper still cannot narrow the catalogue by the attributes you carefully filled in, and all the reader gets is a well-described product they cannot find. Discovery is a pipeline — data, structured output, filtering, search, and the new AI surfaces all read from the same source — and the middle of it is the [collection filters guide](/blogs/shopify-collection-filters-guide).
The goal is a catalogue that is correct. That is useful to every reader of it, known or unknown, and it is the furthest claim the rest of this guide makes.

sections.heading: Where to start if the catalogue is large
paragraphs: Start with the products customers actually buy. The top twenty or thirty SKUs carry most of the discovery, and fixing them first means the audit's results show up in the pages that matter.

Then the product types with the richest attributes — the ones where dimensions, compatibility, and weight actually drive the purchase decision. Those are the products a natural-language request is most likely to target, and the ones where a missing attribute costs the most.

The long tail can wait for a bulk pass, but the standard has to exist before the pass runs: the controlled vocabulary, the required fields, the title shape. A bulk update applied before the standard is defined standardizes the errors instead of removing them, which is the trap the [product data guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) spends most of its length on.

If the gap is measured in thousands of products, a day of external help is usually cheaper than a month of manual edits — the [development service](/shopify-development) page is where that work is scoped. The audit sample in the previous section is the starting point either way.

takeaway: AI discovery does not ask for new tricks; it asks for a catalogue accurate enough to be read. Complete the record, keep availability honest, and every reader — human, filter, or agent — gets the same right answer.

title: Shopify Product Variants Not Working? A Guide to Large Catalogues and Variant Selection
excerpt: Broken selectors, wrong prices, missing images, phantom stock: how variant selection actually works, a top-down troubleshooting path, and what changes when the catalogue gets large.
intro: A customer selects a colour, chooses a size, and expects the price and the product image to update. If the selector breaks — or quietly shows the wrong combination — the product page stops being a reliable buying tool. “Variants not working” is one of the most common problems handed to me, and the good news is that the failure modes are limited and testable. This guide maps the causes, walks a troubleshooting path, and covers what changes when the catalogue stops being small.

sections.heading: What causes Shopify variant selectors to fail?
paragraphs: A variant selector is a small promise: the options the customer picks combine into one purchasable thing, and the page keeps that thing honest. When the promise breaks, the cause is almost always in one of four places — the product data, the theme's selection logic, an app, or rendering at scale.

Data failures are the quiet ones. A variant exists in the admin but never appears as an option on the page because the option mapping is wrong. A size is spelled “L” in one place and “Large” in another, so the selector builds a combination that does not exist. The page looks broken, but the record behind it is what is broken. The [product record note from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-product-data) is a good model of the data side: if the record is complete, the page has something to render.

Theme failures are the loud ones. The selector updates the price but not the image. The add-to-cart button still posts the product's first variant. These are logic errors in how the theme reads the selection — fixable once correctly diagnosed, and exactly the kind of [theme work](/shopify-theme-development) that pays for itself in fewer “checkout is broken” tickets.

App failures are the hardest to attribute, because an inventory sync, a size chart, a personalization script can all touch the same DOM the theme owns. When a selector works in one environment and not another, the app is usually the variable that changed.

sections.heading: Why selected options, prices, images and stock become inconsistent
paragraphs: Every time a customer changes a selection, *five values* on the page must move together: the selected option, the price, the image, the availability state, and the identifier that add-to-cart submits. A broken selector is a page where one of those five stopped performing.

The most common one is the price lag. The selector shows a new selection, the price updates, but the add-to-cart payload still carries the original variant. The customer ends up paying for the wrong thing, or the order arrives wrong, and the bug reads as “checkout is broken” even though checkout did exactly what it was told.

The second is the image. A variant image is optional; when the selected variant has none, the page should fall back to the product's primary image. Themes that assume every variant has an image show a stale or missing picture instead — visually broken, technically a missing default.

The third is availability. A selected variant can be sold out while the product as a whole has stock, and the page must reflect the variant's state, not the product's. If it does not, customers select combinations they cannot buy, and the error surfaces at checkout — the worst place for it to live.

sections.heading: How large variant catalogues change theme behaviour
paragraphs: Most themes are written for the small-catalogue case: a handful of options, a handful of variants, all of them loaded with the product template. That assumption holds until a catalogue stops being small. Shopify's [product variant limit is now 2,048 for all merchants](https://shopify.dev/changelog/posts/the-product-variant-limit-is-now-2048-for-all-merchants), and the platform's [guidance on supporting high-variant products](https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/product-merchandising/variants/support-high-variant-products) exists because the ceiling is not a target.

The practical problems show up in specific ways: a theme that assumes every variant is in `product.variants` works at 12 variants and fails at 800; rendering thousands of hidden option inputs bloats the page; selection logic that re-scans every variant on every click gets slow; filters and search that index variants instead of options start returning noise.

Large catalogues also change what “the product” means. A garment line with eight colours and twelve sizes is not twelve products and eight colours — it is one product with 96 purchasable facts. The [travel-system notes from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-travel-system-details) cover the other side of the same lesson: a travel system that is not a single item. The unit of commerce in Shopify is the variant, and the page has to treat it that way. When a large catalogue's variant prices stop matching the markup they emit, the downstream symptom shows up in the [product schema guide](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors) territory — two records, two readers, one drift.

If your catalogue has hundreds of variants per product, the fix is architectural rather than a patch: selective variant loading, option-level logic, explicit fallbacks. That is a theme change in the real sense — [development work](/shopify-development) worth doing before the next catalogue growth forces it.

sections.heading: How to troubleshoot variant-selection problems
paragraphs: Work top-down: data first, then the page, then the code. Test every option combination, not just the happy path. With two options of three values each that is nine selections, and the bug usually lives in a *corner combination* nobody orders — the largest size in the colour that is almost sold out.

Then check the sold-out and unavailable variants. Select each out-of-stock combination and verify three things: the button state, the availability text, and what add-to-cart actually submits. A page that shows “Sold out” but still posts the variant to the cart has a real bug, even if most customers never see it.

Then the URL and the payload. A selection that survives a page refresh encodes the state in the URL; if the URL says one variant and the page says another, the page is misreading its own state. Open the network tab on add-to-cart and read the request: the variant identifier in that payload is the only ground truth for what the customer will be charged.
What you are verifying at every selection, in the shape that matters (illustrative structure, not a live store export):
sections.code:
# A selection state lives in the URL and the page at once
/product/example-travel-system?variant=45000000000001

# For every selection change, verify all five stay in sync:
#   selected option(s)   the active combination
#   price                that variant's price, never the base price
#   image                the variant image, or the documented fallback
#   availability         that variant's stock state
#   add-to-cart payload  the variant identifier, never the product identifier
sections.codeCaption: THE FIVE VALUES THAT MUST MOVE TOGETHER — ILLUSTRATIVE STRUCTURE

sections.heading: What developers should know about high-variant products
paragraphs: The short version for the person fixing the page: stop assuming `product.variants` contains everything. On a high-variant product it may not, and logic that maps options to variants by scanning the full array is both wrong and slow at scale.

Build selection logic at the option level instead. *Option-level logic* means the customer's choices define a combination, and the theme resolves that combination to a variant, loading only what it needs. Render option values from the product's options, not from an enumerated list of variants. And make the fallbacks explicit: missing variant image, missing variant price, out-of-stock combination. An explicit fallback is a feature; an implicit assumption is a bug waiting for a larger catalogue.

Test against the neighbourhood of the real ceiling. A product with 900 variants is a different system than one with 90 — load time, selector responsiveness, and filter behaviour all change. If the store cannot produce a 900-variant product for testing, a duplicate with synthetic variants is a legitimate stand-in, clearly labelled as such.

The data side needs the same attention, because a high-variant product with inconsistent option values is two bugs wearing one costume — the [product data management guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) covers that half.

sections.heading: A regression checklist for variant changes
paragraphs: Variant changes are high-risk because the blast radius is the whole product page. Any change to options, variants, prices, or images deserves a written pass — the same discipline the [QA checklists](/resources/shopify-qa-checklist) apply to anything customer-facing.

The checklist: every option value renders. Every combination resolves to a real variant. Price, image, and availability update per selection. Sold-out combinations disable add-to-cart. The add-to-cart payload carries the correct variant identifier. The selection survives a refresh. The page still performs at the catalogue's real size. Run it in desktop and mobile, because mobile selectors are often a different implementation wearing the same name.

After the change, watch the signals that a corner combination broke: the refund question about the wrong size, the support email with a screenshot of a missing image. A variant bug that only appears in one corner of the option grid can run quietly for months. The checklist exists so it never gets that far.

sections.heading: When the issue belongs to a theme, app or product-data setup
paragraphs: Once the troubleshooting path is run, the diagnosis splits cleanly. If the admin record is wrong — a missing variant, mismatched option values, a price on the product but not the variant — the fix is in the data, and no theme change helps until the record is correct.

If the record is correct and the page still misbehaves, the fix is in the theme's selection logic. If the page behaves correctly on a clean theme and not on the live one, the fix is in the theme or an app. The *clean-theme test* is the fastest attribution there is, and it is the first thing I do when a store is handed over with “variants not working” as the problem statement.

When an app owns part of the behaviour, the fix may be the app's configuration, removing the app, or making the theme and the app stop fighting over the same element. App-conflict bugs are miserable precisely because the fault line is not visible in any single codebase.
Whatever the attribution, the standard is the same: five values in sync on every selection.

sections.heading: What done looks like
paragraphs: A fixed selector has observable criteria, and they are the same ones the regression checklist checks: every option value renders; every combination — including the corners — resolves to a real variant with the right price, image, and stock state; the add-to-cart payload matches what the page shows; the selection survives a refresh; and it all holds at the catalogue's real size, on desktop and mobile.

If the checklist passes on the 12-variant product but not on the 900-variant one, it is not done — that gap is the large-catalogue section of this guide, and it needs the architectural fix rather than another patch. Stores that also sell through a shopping channel have a fourth witness to check: a variant price that is wrong on the page is the same price that will flag in feed diagnostics, and the [Merchant Center guide](/blogs/shopify-google-merchant-center-errors) is where that side of the evidence is read.

The point of writing the criteria down is that “variants work” is a claim you can verify instead of a feeling you can only hope for. That is the standard I hold a variant fix to before I would call it finished, and it is the standard a store can apply to itself with a browser, a network tab, and an afternoon.

takeaway: A broken variant selector is five values that stopped moving together. Check the data, check the selection state, read the add-to-cart payload — the attribution between data, theme, and app falls out of the evidence.
seoTitle: Shopify Product Variants Not Working? Fix the Causes

title: Shopify Migration SEO Checklist: How to Move Stores Without Losing Important URLs
excerpt: A migration can look perfect on launch day and still lose the URLs a store spent years earning. The inventory, the mapping, the redirects, and the post-launch checks, in the order I run them.
intro: A redesign can look perfect on launch day and still cost the store the URLs it spent years earning — the backlink from a magazine article, the collection page that ranked for a money keyword, the product URL customers bookmarked, the blog post other sites cite for its fitting advice. The failure is rarely a crash. It is a *silent retirement*: the URL stops existing, nothing tells anyone, and the signal it carried evaporates. This guide is the checklist I run before and after a move: inventory, mapping, redirects, and the post-launch verification that shows what actually made it through.

sections.heading: What can go wrong during a Shopify migration?
paragraphs: The visible store is the easy part. What breaks is what nobody sees on launch day: a backlink now hitting a 404, a collection that ranked for a money keyword and is gone, an old product URL that regular customers still bookmark. A month later the store looks slower and smaller in search than the old one did, and nobody can say when it started.

The second failure mode is the messy redirect: a chain (A to B to C), a redirect to the wrong target, a 302 used where a 301 was meant. These work fine in the browser until you need the full signal transferred, and the difference matters. [Shopify's redirect documentation](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/menus-and-links/url-redirect) is the primary reference on the Shopify side, and [Google's technical requirements for search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/technical) is what the destination side has to satisfy.
The checklist below exists so that neither failure mode gets a quiet moment.

sections.heading: Build a URL inventory before changing the store
paragraphs: Before anything moves, list everything that exists. The inventory has four rows per store: products with their canonical URLs, collections, pages and blog posts, and — the row that gets forgotten — image and asset URLs that other pages and feeds reference.

The honest sources are three, and they answer different questions. The old site's sitemap tells you what the store declared. A crawl tells you what is reachable. Search Console tells you which of those URLs were actually earning impressions and clicks. A map built from the sitemap alone will miss the URLs that only backlinks and bookmarks know about, which are often exactly the ones worth keeping alive.

For each URL, record what it is, where it points, and — where the data exists — how it performs. *The performance column* is what separates a technical exercise from a business decision: the URL that drives a third of organic orders gets a better destination and more scrutiny than the one that has not seen a click in two years.

This is the step that gets skipped under deadline pressure, and it is the step that turns every later step into guesswork. A store migrating through a [Shopify development engagement](/shopify-development) should treat the inventory as the first deliverable, because it defines what “done” means at the end.

sections.heading: Map old URLs to the most relevant new destinations
paragraphs: Every old URL gets one of four decisions: a 301 to its best new destination, a 301 to a category or landing page when no single equivalent exists, an intentional 404 when the content is genuinely gone, or a written note explaining why it was left alone. The discipline is that every URL in the inventory gets a decision — an unmapped URL is not “no problem,” it is an unexamined one.

The mapping rule: the destination must be the most relevant page, not the closest page. A renamed product redirects to the renamed product. A discontinued line redirects to the collection that replaced it. A blog post whose content moved redirects to the page that now carries that content. Redirecting everything to the homepage is the classic shortcut, and it quietly taxes every URL it touches.

sections.heading: How to create and validate Shopify redirects
paragraphs: Shopify creates redirects from the admin and imports them from CSV at scale. One row per source, one target per source, and the redirect type said plainly: 301 when the old page is retired and the signal should move, 302 when the move is temporary.

Validation is where the plan meets reality. For a sample of the mapping — and for every URL that mattered in the inventory — request the old URL and read the response: a *single 301*, straight to the final destination, ending in a 200. A chain of two or three hops is a bug in the plan even if the browser never complains; chains dilute the signal and they rot.

Also check what Shopify cannot redirect cleanly. Some path types behave differently — the platform's own [redirect documentation](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/menus-and-links/url-redirect) lists which URL types can be redirected and how — so the plan must know which rows are platform-supported and which need a different mechanism, such as handling at the domain or CDN layer.
After the import, re-crawl the old URLs. That crawl result is the evidence: every mapped URL resolving in one hop to a live destination is the row that gets ticked.

sections.heading: Product, collection, blog and image URL checks
paragraphs: Products: the new product's URL should be the stable one the store intends to keep. If the handle changed, the old handle gets a redirect. If the product moved between collections, the product URL itself should not have changed — that is a collection problem, not a product one.

Collections: a renamed or restructured collection is often the highest-value redirect row in the plan, because collections are where the URLs that earn category search traffic live. The [collection SEO notes from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-collection-seo) cover why the collection itself — not just the products in it — is the SEO surface, which is exactly why its URL deserves the best destination available.

Blog posts: the posts other sites link to get individual redirects to their new homes. Posts whose content was merged redirect to the merged page. A blog being shut down entirely still needs its top posts mapped — those are the URLs with backlinks on them.

Images: the most neglected row. Old image URLs referenced by backlinks, feeds, or pages that were not updated will 404 unless the assets moved with their paths. The check is simple: request a sample of old image URLs and confirm they resolve. Image URLs that die are how a migration leaks broken layouts onto other people's pages.

sections.heading: What to test before DNS changes and launch
paragraphs: The pre-launch pass runs on the new store *behind the old DNS*: every redirect row tested (the sample plus all high-value rows), every key page on the new store checked for a 200, a canonical tag, and the content it should have, and the new sitemap published and complete.

Then the cross-checks: internal links on the new store point to new URLs, not stale handles; search and filter URLs work; checkout completes an order on the new store. The DNS switch itself is the boring part, and the verification after it is where the migration is actually won or lost.

One check specific to migrations: the new store's pages must be eligible for indexing on their own. Redirects do not fix a destination that is blocked, canonicalized to the wrong host, or thin. If the old URL redirects to a new page Google cannot or will not index, the signal has nowhere to land — that is the failure mode the [pages-not-indexed guide](/blogs/shopify-pages-not-indexed-google) walks through step by step.

Structured data needs the same pre-launch attention: product and page markup must be correct on the new URLs before launch, so the first crawl of the new store sees consistent data. Doing it after launch means starting with a backlog of mismatches already accumulating — the [product schema guide](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors) is the reference for that pass.

sections.heading: Post-launch monitoring in Google Search Console
paragraphs: The Search Console property for the migrating domain is the owner's to connect and read — it is an account decision I do not make on the owner's behalf. Here is what I would look for, and when.

In the first two weeks: URL Inspection for the high-value redirects. The old URL inspected should show the redirect; the destination inspected should show indexed, or at least a valid candidate. In the coverage report, the new URLs should be arriving, and the old URLs should show as redirected rather than as errors with nothing behind them.

In the first month: impressions and clicks for the pages that mattered. The realistic expectation is that numbers dip and recover — a migration is a controlled shock, and the recovery curve is the metric of success. A URL that ranked before launch and never recovers is a row in the inventory that needs a second look at its destination.

After that, the standing habit: keep the Search Console data as the living audit of the redirect plan. Three months out, the URLs still failing are the ones the plan got wrong — and they are cheap to fix while the mapping is still fresh.

sections.heading: Common redirect mistakes and recovery steps
paragraphs: Redirect chains and loops: a redirect pointing to another old URL, or two URLs redirecting at each other. Recovery is mechanical — flatten every chain to a single hop, and a re-crawl finds what remains.

The 302 that was meant to be a 301: temporary redirects set up during staging that never got switched. Audit the redirect table for 302s older than the launch and decide each one deliberately — flip it or retire it.

The homepage catch-all: every unmapped URL landing on the homepage, diluting it and burying the real destinations. Go back through the inventory and give the unmapped rows real decisions, even when the decision is a deliberate 404.

The destination that was never checked: the redirect is perfect and the page it points to is thin, blocked, or canonicalized away. Fix the destination — a redirect is only as good as the page that keeps it. A migration done well is a store whose old URLs still work, on purpose, after launch.

takeaway: The store that survives a migration is not the one with the best launch day — it is the one whose inventory was complete, whose redirects were single-hop, and whose destinations were verified after the switch.
seoTitle: Shopify Migration SEO Checklist: Redirects and Launch Checks
seoDescription: Moving to Shopify? Use this migration SEO checklist to map URLs, plan redirects, check important pages and monitor technical issues after launch.

title: Shopify Markets SEO: Languages, Currencies, Hreflang and Duplicate URLs
excerpt: A wrong-currency product page is a translation problem and a configuration problem at once. How Markets organizes international storefronts, what hreflang actually does, and the audit before a market goes live.
intro: If a customer in France lands on an English product page with the wrong currency, the problem is bigger than translation. The store has to communicate which version belongs to which market — to people and to search engines — and a wrong price shown is a wrong price sold. International stores are where configuration errors become customer-facing errors fast. This guide covers how Shopify Markets is meant to work, where the seams are, and the audit I run before a market goes live.

sections.heading: How Shopify Markets organizes international storefronts
paragraphs: Markets is Shopify's model for selling to different countries and language groups from one store. Each market carries its own currency, shipping zones, and payment methods — and, for SEO, its own URL structure and language. *One catalogue, many storefronts*, each with a clear identity.

The SEO-relevant part is that Shopify generates the international signals when configured properly: market-specific URLs, canonical tags that point each market version at itself, and [hreflang annotations](https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/seo/hreflang) that tell search engines which language and region a page serves. [Shopify's international SEO documentation for Markets](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/markets/seo) is the primary reference for how these pieces are intended to fit together.

“When configured properly” is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Markets removes most of the manual work, but it does not remove the failure modes: a market that exists in the shipping settings but not in the URL structure, a language selector that writes one state while the page says another, a theme that renders extra hreflang tags on top of the platform's own. The platform generates the signals; the configuration decides whether they agree.

docRefs.note: Shopify's merchant documentation for how Markets handles hreflang, canonical URLs and market-specific sitemaps — the first stop for the intended behaviour.

docRefs.title: Hreflang (Shopify theme developer docs)
docRefs.note: The developer-side reference for how hreflang tags are emitted on theme pages, including what a theme can and cannot change.

sections.heading: Subfolders vs. subdomains vs. country-code domains
paragraphs: The URL question — shop.example.com/fr/, example.com/fr/, or example.fr — is a decision with real consequences, and it is the one merchants most often want to reverse after launch.

Subfolders under the primary domain are the pattern Shopify's Markets is built around, and the one with the least moving parts: one domain, market sitemaps, canonicals that stay on one host. For most stores they are the right default, and they are what the platform's tooling assumes.

Subdomains and country-code domains carry their own weight: separate DNS, sometimes separate Search Console properties and analytics views, more places for the configuration to drift. If a store already lives on ccdoms for brand reasons, that is defensible — but then every market's signals (canonical, hreflang, sitemap, robots) must be verified per host, because the platform's defaults stop covering you.

Choose the structure before the first market launch, not after. Changing it later is a [migration](/blogs/shopify-migration-seo-checklist) in disguise: every old market URL becomes a redirect row, and every signal has to be rebuilt.

sections.heading: What hreflang does — and what it does not do
paragraphs: Hreflang is a recommendation, not a command. It tells a search engine: these pages serve the same content to different languages and regions, and here is the mapping. When the mapping is correct and consistent — page A in French points to page B in English, and page B points back to page A — search engines can serve the right version to the right user.

What it does not do: create the versions, translate content, or guarantee any ranking. And the big one — it does not fix inconsistent pages. If the French page and the English page have different prices, different availability, or different content, hreflang is annotating a discrepancy rather than resolving it.

The *symmetry* requirement is where most implementations break. Hreflang is a graph: every tag you emit is a promise that the target page points back. A one-way annotation is a half-promise, and search engines treat broken mappings as noise. The audit below checks symmetry explicitly, because it is the check that catches the most real-world damage.

sections.heading: Canonical URLs across translated product pages
paragraphs: Every market version of a product page should carry a *self-canonical* — a canonical tag pointing at its own URL in its own market. The failure mode is the accidental cross-canonical: the French product page carrying a canonical that points at the English one, telling search engines the French page is a duplicate to be discarded.

That failure is usually a configuration or theme problem, not a content problem. A market missing from the URL structure produces pages the platform cannot canonicalize correctly. A theme that hardcodes the canonical to the primary market overwrites the platform's own output. Either way the page keeps loading and keeps selling while telling search engines it does not exist.

The check is two lines per page: read the canonical tag in the page source and confirm it equals the page's own URL in its own market. Run it across a sample of products in every market before launch, and re-run it after any theme or market change. It is cheap, deterministic, and it catches the most expensive class of international bug. What correct market tags look like, illustratively:

<!-- Illustrative output, modelled on the structure Shopify's
     Markets documentation describes. The point is the relationship:
     each market page canonicalizes to itself, and hreflang is symmetric. -->

<!-- French product page -->
<link rel="canonical" href="https://shop.example.com/fr/products/example-chair" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr-fr" href="https://shop.example.com/fr/products/example-chair" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en"    href="https://shop.example.com/en/products/example-chair" />

<!-- English product page -->
<link rel="canonical" href="https://shop.example.com/en/products/example-chair" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en"    href="https://shop.example.com/en/products/example-chair" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="fr-fr" href="https://shop.example.com/fr/products/example-chair" />
sections.codeCaption: WHAT CORRECT MARKET TAGS LOOK LIKE — ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT A LIVE STORE

sections.heading: How localized content differs from direct translation
paragraphs: A translated product title is a start, not a finish. Localization means the page answers the market's question in that market's terms: units (kilograms, not pounds), sizes (the EU scale, not US), legal phrasing, payment expectations, and the vocabulary that market actually searches for.

The SEO-visible difference: a direct translation keeps the source market's keywords, which the target market may never type. A localized page uses the phrasing that market's searchers use — which is the difference between a page that earns impressions and a perfect translation nobody finds.

The boundary: I do not translate. Localization is a content decision the store makes with someone who knows the market; my part is making sure the technical layer — URLs, canonicals, hreflang, sitemaps — does not undermine the content once it is written. A beautifully localized page on a broken hreflang graph is a page search engines cannot place.

For stores in multiple markets, the [collection-level SEO work](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-collection-seo) has to happen per market as well: a collection that works in English may need a different structure, or a different name, to work in French.

sections.heading: How to audit market URLs, currencies and language selectors
paragraphs: The audit runs per market, in a fixed order. First, the URL: load the market's homepage and a sample of products, and confirm the URL is the market's own — not the primary market's with a query parameter doing the work.

Second, the currency: confirm the displayed currency matches the market's configured currency, and that the currency selector, when used, lands on the market's own URLs rather than a session-only switch.

Third, the language selector: pick a market and verify the URL changes to the market's structure. A selector that changes the page without changing the URL is the *classic red flag* — the customer sees French, the page is still the English URL, and every signal says English.

Fourth, the tags: canonical self-referencing in each market, hreflang present and symmetric, and the market's pages in the sitemap. Fifth, the data: prices and availability rendered per market. The audit is a set of deterministic checks, which is what makes it repeatable — run it before launch, after every theme deploy, and whenever a market's configuration changes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes, including duplicate hreflang output
paragraphs: The double-emitted hreflang: a theme, an app, or a snippet someone added in 2024 renders its own hreflang tags on top of the platform's. Two sets of annotations on one page is contradictory noise, and it is the mistake I see most often in international audits. The fix is finding every emitter and leaving exactly one — usually the platform's.

The market that exists in shipping but not in SEO: it ships and sells, but its URLs were never part of the structure, so its pages are the primary market's pages with a currency override. The fix is configuring the market's URL structure and re-running the canonical check.
The broken symmetry: half the hreflang graph points one way. The fix is a symmetry check across a product sample in every market pair — mechanical, and decisive.

Auditing the primary market only: the primary market is configured first and configured best, and every other market is where the drift lives. If the audit covered one market, it covered the easiest one.

sections.heading: International SEO launch checklist
paragraphs: Before a market goes live, in order: the market's URL structure configured and loading its own pages; canonical tags self-referencing in that market; hreflang present, symmetric, and emitted once; the market's pages in the sitemap; currency and price rendering verified on a product sample; the language selector landing on market URLs; and the content decision documented — which pages are localized, which are translated, and which are intentionally the primary-market version. When the gaps in that list are theme-level ones, they are [development work](/shopify-development) in the normal sense: a scoped change with a verification pass, not a configuration toggle.

After launch: the Search Console property for the relevant domain, checking that the market's URLs are being crawled and indexed. Indexing is its own stage — a correctly configured market whose URLs never get indexed is a configuration problem that looks like an SEO problem, and the [pages-not-indexed guide](/blogs/shopify-pages-not-indexed-google) is where that diagnosis runs.

The standing habit: one market's worth of the audit per quarter, rotating through the markets, so no market's drift gets older than a quarter. International stores fail slowly — one wrong canonical at a time — and the rotation is what keeps the failure from becoming the default.

takeaway: Hreflang is a graph of promises between versions of the same page. Verify the promises — self-canonical, symmetric annotations, one emitter, market-owned URLs — and the international store stops fighting its own configuration.
seoTitle: Shopify Markets SEO: Hreflang and International URLs
seoDescription: Learn how Shopify Markets handles international SEO, language URLs, hreflang, canonicals and localized content—and what to check before launch.

title: Shopify Product Schema Errors: How to Check Price, Availability and Product Data
excerpt: When the page shows one price and the markup says another, the page has two conflicting records. How to inspect, validate, and fix product structured data — without adding a second schema on top.
intro: You update a product's price and stock status in Shopify, but the page's structured data still shows something different. That mismatch undermines the consistency of what search systems read from the page — and it is one of the most checkable problems in storefront SEO, because the evidence is on the page itself. This guide is the diagnostic path: what the markup is supposed to say, how to read what actually shipped, and how to fix the mismatch without layering a second schema on top.

sections.heading: What product structured data communicates
paragraphs: Product structured data is the machine-readable summary a product page ships with: the product's name, its price, the currency, its availability, and the offer those values belong to. Search systems read it as the page's own account of what is for sale, at what price, and whether it can be bought right now.

The word to hold onto is summary. The markup is not a source of truth — it is *a rendering of the truth*, generated from the product's live data. When the summary disagrees with the page a customer reads, the page has two conflicting records, and every system that reads the markup inherits the discrepancy.

That is also why schema problems are fixable in a way most SEO problems are not. The check is deterministic: read the rendered price, read the markup's price, compare. Read the availability, read the markup's availability, compare. A mismatch is a bug with a location, and the job is finding which layer produced the wrong value.

sections.heading: Product, Offer, price, currency and availability
paragraphs: The shape that matters is the relationship: a Product holds an Offer, the Offer carries the price, the price carries a currency, and the availability states whether the offer can be acted on right now. Get any of those wrong and the summary is wrong in a specific, checkable way.

The currency is the one that gets skipped. A price without a currency, or with the wrong one, is a number a system cannot safely use — and on a store selling to several markets, the wrong currency is the international version of the same bug. The [Markets guide](/blogs/shopify-markets-international-seo) covers the market structure; this is where it becomes a data problem.

Availability is *a state, not a label*: in stock, out of stock, preorder, sold out. The markup should carry the state the page is showing. A discounted product whose sale has ended but whose markup still carries a sale price is a mismatch that survives until someone checks.
The shape of a correct product record, with illustrative values — the structure is the point:
sections.codeCaption: THE RECORD, AS IT SHOULD READ — ILLUSTRATIVE VALUES

sections.heading: Why Shopify themes and apps can produce conflicting markup
paragraphs: Three layers can touch the product markup, and any one of them can produce a wrong value. The theme renders the page and often emits the schema. An app can inject its own product markup — reviews, subscriptions, size charts — and occasionally injects a second, stale product block. And the data itself changes: a price updated in the admin, a sale that started and ended, a variant that went out of stock.

The classic failure is *staleness at the seam*. The theme's schema is generated once from the data it had when it rendered, and the price changed after that. Or an app's block was written for last year's data shape and quietly emits the old price. When the rendered page and the markup disagree, one of the three layers drifted.

The second classic is duplication: two product blocks on one page, one from the theme and one from an app, with different values. A system reading that page encounters two answers and picks whichever it parses first — which is not a strategy you can rely on. The [Merchant Center guide](/blogs/shopify-google-merchant-center-errors) covers the downstream version of the problem, where the feed and the page disagree and the shopping channel has to pick a side.

sections.heading: How to inspect rendered HTML and JSON-LD
paragraphs: The inspection takes two minutes per product and settles the diagnosis. Open the product page, open the page source, and find the structured data — the JSON-LD script blocks in the head, or the microdata in the body. Read the Product block: name, price, currency, availability, and the offer's URL.

Then read the page the customer sees: the title, the price, the currency symbol, the availability state, the add-to-cart button. Compare field by field. A mismatch now has a location — a specific value on a specific layer — and the fix starts from evidence instead of suspicion.

The same pass covers what customers do not see but search systems do: the title tag, the canonical, the image references inside the markup. Google's [structured data guidance for merchants](https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7331077) sets the standard for what the data must agree with, and its [image documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-images) covers the image side — discoverable image elements, useful alt text, the context the image sits in.

Do this on a sample that includes the *edge cases*: the product mid-sale, the product with a sold-out variant, the product that changed price this week. The middle of the catalogue is where the schema is boring; the edges are where it lies.

docRefs.title: Google Images best practices (Google for Developers)
docRefs.note: The guidance on discoverable image elements, useful alt text and page context — the image half of the product record.

sections.heading: Test variant URLs and sale-price changes
paragraphs: The base product page is the easy case. The test that catches real bugs is the variant URL: load a specific variant and check that the markup's offer matches that variant's price and availability, not the product's first variant's. A page that always reports the first variant's price is a bug that only shows up in the combinations customers actually buy.

Then the sale test: start a sale on a test product, read the markup, end the sale, read it again. The markup should move with the state — sale price while the sale is live, regular price after. A store whose markup lags its own sales cycles is feeding stale numbers to every reader of its pages, and the lag is the measurement you need to fix.

Third, the stock flip: take a variant out of stock, reload, check the availability in the markup; put it back, reload, check again. Availability that does not move with reality ends in customers ordering what cannot ship — a schema problem that has become a fulfilment problem.

None of this needs special tooling. A browser, the page source, and a product you are willing to change are the whole setup — which is the point: the check is deterministic, and a deterministic check is a check you can repeat on every deploy.

sections.heading: Validate structured data and Merchant Center feeds
paragraphs: Once the rendered page and the markup agree, the second audience is the shopping channels. Merchant Center reads both the feed your store publishes and the page's structured data, and its diagnostics flag where they disagree — which makes it a useful independent witness, because it is a system you do not operate checking your work.

The feed and the page are two renderings of the same record, and they can drift: the feed generated daily, the page rendered live, a price change landing between the two. When the diagnostics flag a price or availability mismatch, the question is not which side is wrong — it is which side is stale, and the fix is making the generation and the rendering read the same source at the same time.

I do not connect a store's Merchant Center on the owner's behalf, and the diagnostics are the owner's to read — but the reading is specific: note the flagged field, the flagged product, and the two values, then run the inspection above on that product. The diagnostic tells you where to look; the page source tells you what is true. The full workflow for that loop is in the [Merchant Center errors guide](/blogs/shopify-google-merchant-center-errors).

sections.heading: Fix mismatches without adding duplicate schema
paragraphs: The instinct when a product page's schema looks wrong is to add a corrected block alongside it — a second JSON-LD with the right values. That is how a page ends up with two Product blocks and a system that reads whichever it parses first. The fix is correcting the emitter, not adding a rival.

So the fix order matters. Find the layer that produces the wrong value — the theme's schema generation, an app's injected block, or a data problem upstream — and fix it there. If an app owns the markup, the fix is the app's configuration or the app itself. If the theme owns it, the fix is the template that generates the block. A patch block on top is a fix that creates the next bug.

When the markup is correct but sparse — no images, no reviews, no brand — the move is to fill the record, not to overclaim. A product schema that says exactly what the page says, and says it once, is worth more than a richer schema that disagrees with the page in one field.

sections.heading: A repeatable product-schema QA checklist
paragraphs: The checklist is the inspection above, written down so it survives the deploy that would otherwise re-break it. For a sample of products including the edge cases: price matches, currency matches, availability matches, the offer URL is the product's own URL, the variant URL reports the variant's values, the sale state moves with the sale, and there is exactly one Product block on the page.

Run it after any change that touches prices, inventory, themes, or product apps — those are the changes that move the data under a static schema. A store with the habit in place finds the mismatch on the deploy that introduced it; a store without it finds it in the Merchant Center diagnostics a month later, when the deploy is a memory.

When the check says the data underneath is the problem — a price in two places, an availability that does not match the stock — no schema can fix it, because the schema is faithfully reporting a broken record. That is the [product data management guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management), and it is where this checklist points when the answer is the data, not the markup. For stores where the schema layer needs real engineering — a theme that generates the block wrong, an app that needs replacing — that is [development work](/shopify-development), and it has a verifiable before and after: the page and its markup, agreeing.

takeaway: Product schema is the page's word to the machines that read it. The check is deterministic — rendered value versus markup value — and the fix is correcting the emitter, never adding a rival block.
seoTitle: Shopify Product Schema: Fix Structured Data Errors

title: Shopify Collection Filters Not Working? A Guide to Search, Sorting and Product Discovery
excerpt: Filters are where catalogue data quality becomes visible: every inconsistent attribute shows up as a filter that fails. How filters should behave, why they go empty or wrong, and the QA pass that keeps them honest.
intro: A customer knows the colour, size, or price range they want. If the collection page makes them scroll through every product — or a filter returns the wrong results — the store has made an easy decision feel difficult. Filters are where the catalogue's data quality becomes visible, because every inconsistent attribute shows up as a filter that fails. This guide covers how filters should behave, why they go missing, empty, or wrong, and the QA pass that keeps them honest — on desktop and in the mobile drawer, where most of the filtering actually happens.

sections.heading: How collection filters should work
paragraphs: A filter makes a claim: if you select “Navy”, everything shown has a colour that is genuinely Navy — recorded in the catalogue, not guessed by the page. The customer's mental model is simple and correct, and the store's job is to make the model true.

The behaviour contract has four parts. The options shown must match what the catalogue actually contains — no option for a size nobody sells, and no product hiding behind an option that is not offered. The results must respond: selecting a filter changes the grid, the count updates, and combined filters narrow correctly. The selected state must be visible, so the customer can see what is applied. And the escape must be one action away: a reset that clears the state without losing the customer's place in the store.

Filter bugs are rarely filter bugs. When a filter returns the wrong products, the mechanism is doing exactly what it was told with a catalogue that says something different from the truth. The fix is usually the data — which is also what makes it worth fixing properly.

sections.heading: Filters vs. sorting vs. on-site search
paragraphs: The three discovery tools do different jobs, and stores that blur them confuse customers. Filtering narrows by attribute: colour, size, price band, material. Sorting orders by a dimension: newest, price, best selling. Search answers a question in the customer's words, which may not map to any attribute at all.

The failure mode is overlap without coordination. A customer searches “navy” and gets a results page with no filters — the search found the colour, but the page cannot narrow it, and the customer is back at square one. Or the filter offers “Navy” as a colour while the search treats “navy” as a free-text match against titles — two different answers to the same question, from the same store.

The coordination is a data decision: the attributes that power the filters are the same attributes the search indexes, and both read from the same catalogue records. The three tools are three views of one pipeline, and the [AI discovery guide](/blogs/shopify-ai-search-product-discovery) makes the same point from the other direction — the cleaner the attributes, the more tools can read them correctly.

sections.heading: Why filters can be missing, empty or inaccurate
paragraphs: Missing filters: the attribute exists in the data but not in the filter configuration — a catalogue full of materials that the collection page never offers as a filter. Compare the attributes the products carry against the options the page exposes, and the gap is the missing filter. Closing it is a configuration decision, not a code change.

Empty filters: the option exists but selects nothing — or selects the wrong things. This is the data-inconsistency signature. “Navy”, “Navy Blue”, “Dark Navy”, and “navy” are four values to the filter engine and one colour to the customer; a filter built on the raw values has five options, and *the empty option* is the catalogue telling you, in its own UI, that the data is not standardized.

Inaccurate filters: the option selects products that do not carry the attribute, or misses ones that do. The causes: the attribute entered in free text instead of the controlled field, a metafield set on some products and not others, an app mapping the attribute its own way. Each cause points at a different layer — the data entry, the field definition, the app — and the [product data management guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) is where those layers get sorted out.

One note for stores that have lived with this: filter problems are not a reason to remove filtering. A collection that cannot be narrowed makes every customer do the store's job. The [navigation notes from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-navigation) cover the structure that brings customers to the collection; the filters are what make the collection do its job once they are there.

sections.heading: Product tags, metafields and consistent product attributes
paragraphs: The right first question is not the mechanism but the location: where does the attribute live? The answer carries the weight.

Product options and their values are the platform's structured fields — a size is a value of the Size option, and the filter reads them directly. Tags are the flexible-but-loose option: free-form, untyped, and only as consistent as the person who typed them. Tags power a lot of filter setups, and they rot in the way tags rot. If the store's filtering rides on tags, the standardization work in the [product data guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) is the prerequisite, not the follow-up.

Metafields and metaobjects are the structured alternative: a defined field with a type and, where needed, a *controlled set of values* — the catalogue's own vocabulary, enforced by the field rather than by discipline. For the attributes the store cares about — material, compatibility, care instructions — a metaobject is the difference between “filters work because nobody typed it wrong yet” and “filters work because the field cannot be typed wrong.”
The decision rule I use: if the attribute powers a filter, a comparison, or a feed, it deserves a structured field. If it is a label for the team, a tag is fine.

sections.heading: Configure and test Shopify Search & Discovery
paragraphs: Shopify's [Search & Discovery app](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/online-store/search-and-discovery) is where the store configures what search and filters actually see: which fields are searchable, which attributes become filter facets, how the results respond. The configuration is the contract between the catalogue and the discovery layer, and it is worth reading in full before you are surprised by it.

The test is behavioural, not configurational. Pick ten products across the catalogue's range and verify each one: it appears under every filter it should satisfy, it does not appear under the ones it should not, and a combination of two filters narrows to the intersection. The store's own collection pages are the test bench — and a second storefront's listing shows the same configuration against a different catalogue shape, which is what the inline image below shows.

Performance belongs in the test too, because a filter that takes two seconds to respond is a filter customers stop using. Shopify's [theme performance guidance](https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/best-practices/performance) is the reference for why filtering on large collections is a theme-side cost — and why the fix sometimes belongs in the theme rather than the app settings.

When the configuration is right and the behaviour is still wrong, the attribution is usually upstream: the data the configuration reads. That is the pattern across this whole guide, and it is why discovery work on the [Shopify development](/shopify-development) side is a data project with a UI, not the reverse.

sections.heading: Mobile filter drawers, selected states and reset controls
paragraphs: Most of a store's filtering happens in a drawer on a phone, and the drawer is a different implementation from the desktop sidebar — same contract, different surface. The test path is the same (does selecting narrow correctly?), but the failure modes are mobile-specific: a drawer that does not show the selected state, a grid that does not update behind the drawer, a count that updates one selection late.

The *selected state* is where mobile filtering breaks most visibly. A customer who cannot see which filters are applied is navigating blind: they select “Navy”, the grid changes, they select “Under $100”, the grid changes again, and there is no record of what they have done. Applied filters need to be visible at a glance — chips above the grid, or marked options in the drawer.

Reset needs to be one tap back to the full collection for the customer who has filtered themselves into a dead end — Navy, under $50, and the discontinued line. A reset that only clears some filters, or that leaves the collection page, is a small frustration that compounds: the customer learns the filters are unreliable and starts scrolling instead.

The drawer also has a layout job: tappable options, long attribute values that wrap or truncate sensibly, and no trapped scroll. None of it is glamorous, and all of it is the difference between a drawer customers use and one they give up on.

sections.heading: When filter URLs should — and should not — be indexable
paragraphs: A filtered collection often has its own URL, the filter state encoded in the query string. That URL raises a question the unfiltered page never does: should search engines index it?

The case for indexing: a filter that represents a genuinely distinct, well-stocked view — “all travel systems under $800” — is a page a customer might want to land on, and a search engine might reasonably rank. The case against is the combinatorial explosion: twelve filters of four values each is 4,096 URLs, most of them thin, most of them near-duplicates of each other, most of them a filter state no customer asked for. Indexed, they dilute the store's crawl budget and create a long tail of low-value pages that the [indexing guide](/blogs/shopify-pages-not-indexed-google) would spend its whole diagnosis explaining.

The rule I apply: *the base collection page is the indexable unit*. A filter view is indexable only if it is curated — a real, maintained, well-stocked view the store would stand behind as a page — and even then the store says so deliberately, not by accident of the URL structure. The uncurated filter states get told not to be indexed, which is not hiding anything: it is telling search engines the collection page is the page.

This is the same discipline as the [collection SEO notes](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-collection-seo): the collection is the SEO surface, and every derivative view either earns its own standing or defers to it.

sections.heading: Collection-filter QA checklist
paragraphs: The checklist runs per collection, in order, and it ends with the data. First, the options: every filter offered is populated, every option has results, and no option is an empty promise. Second, the narrowing: a single filter changes the grid correctly, two filters intersect correctly, and the count matches the grid.

Third, the state: the selected filters are visible on desktop and in the mobile drawer, and the reset clears everything in one action while keeping the customer on the collection. Fourth, the edge cases: a filter that matches exactly one product, a filter combined with a price sort, and a filter applied just before a new product is added to the collection — does the new product appear, and under the right options?

Fifth, performance: the filter responds without a visible pause at the collection's real size, on a mid-range phone on cellular — not a studio laptop on fibre. Sixth, the data: pick the three most-filtered attributes and check how consistently they are recorded across a sample of the catalogue. The checklist ends where the guide started, with the record — because the record is what the filter's claim is made on.

And the habit: run the checklist after any catalogue import, any attribute change, and any theme deploy — the three events that move the data under a working filter. A store that treats filtering as configured-and-done will discover, from its customers' impatience, that the filters were never done at all.

takeaway: A filter is the catalogue's word made interactive. The options must match the data, the state must stay visible, the reset must be one tap, and the data must be standardized enough that the word is true.
seoTitle: Shopify Collection Filters: Setup and Troubleshooting
seoDescription: Learn how to troubleshoot Shopify collection filters, improve product attributes, test mobile filtering and make product discovery easier.

title: Shopify Pages Not Indexed by Google? A Practical Troubleshooting Checklist
excerpt: A published page that never appears in search is usually an access problem, not a content problem. The stages in order — access, crawl, index — with the evidence to check at each one.
intro: You publish a new product, collection, or article, search for it on Google, and find nothing. Before changing the title or rewriting the page, check whether Google can access, crawl, and index the URL at all — because a page that is not indexed is an access problem, not a content problem. This guide walks the stages in the order they should be checked, and covers the case that the checklists underprepare for: a perfectly valid page that still stays quiet.

sections.heading: Crawling, indexing and ranking are different stages
paragraphs: The first move is to name the stage where the page actually stopped. Crawling is Google arriving at the URL and reading it. Indexing is the decision to keep the page in the index so it can appear in results. Ranking is what happens after — and it is not this problem. A page that is not indexed has not lost a ranking fight; it never got into the room.

The distinction matters because the instinct response to “my page is not on Google” is to rewrite the page — better title, better copy, more keywords. That is fixing the ranking stage for a page that failed the access stage, and the rewrite changes nothing. Each stage has its own evidence, and this checklist checks them in order, starting with the stage that most often fails and least often gets checked.

One more thing to hold from the start: meeting the technical requirements does not guarantee indexing. A page can be accessible, crawlable, well-canonicalized, and sitemapped — and still not get indexed, because the index is a decision, not a mirror. The checklist gets you to “the page is eligible and I have asked,” which is the furthest any store can legitimately go.

docRefs.title: Technical requirements for search (Google)
docRefs.note: Google's reference for what a page must satisfy to be eligible for indexing: accessible to Googlebot, a successful HTTP response, and indexable content.

docRefs.title: Build a sitemap (Google)
docRefs.note: The sitemap guidance — what sitemaps help search engines discover, and the explicit note that submitting one does not guarantee crawling or indexing.

sections.heading: Start with URL Inspection in Search Console
paragraphs: The Search Console property for the store's domain is the owner's to connect — an account decision I do not make on the owner's behalf — but the reading of it is specific, and it is the fastest way to name the stage. The URL Inspection tool takes one URL and reports what Google knows about it: whether it is indexed, whether Google can access it, which canonical it chose, and whether a validation has been requested.

The labels in the tool change over time — Google has renamed and regrouped these states more than once — so read the substance rather than memorizing the label. “Indexed” means the page is in the index. A state describing a page Google saw but did not select, usually with a reason (duplicate, canonical choice, low quality), means the page was crawled and the decision went the other way — a different problem with a different fix. A state describing an access failure means the page was never read, and that is the checklist's first stop.

One URL Inspection per failing page, with the page's own URL entered exactly as it should exist. If the inspection says indexed but the site: search still shows nothing, that is the waiting-on-a-decision territory the [migration guide](/blogs/shopify-migration-seo-checklist) discusses for new stores: indexed does not instantly mean surfaced. If the inspection says not indexed, the rest of this checklist is the path, in the order it should be run.

sections.heading: Check HTTP status, robots directives and canonical URLs
paragraphs: The *access layer* has three deterministic checks, all visible in the page's own output. First, the HTTP status: the page must return a successful response — a 200, not a 404, not a 5xx, not a soft block. A page that 404s for Googlebot because of a redirect loop or a blocked path is a closed door, not a content problem.

Second, the robots directives: both the robots.txt that governs crawling and the meta robots tag on the page itself. A noindex on the meta, a Disallow on the path, or a robots.txt that blocks the whole agent — each is a deliberate signal that the page should not be indexed, and each is found by reading the actual output rather than guessing at the setting.

Third, the canonical tag: the page should canonicalize to itself. A page that canonicalizes to another URL is telling search engines it is a duplicate of that other page — a complete explanation for why it is not indexed, and one of the most common findings in this whole checklist, especially after a migration or a platform change that rewrote the URLs.

Here is the access layer as this journal's own production site publishes it — the robots.txt in full, and one of this journal's article pages showing its own robots meta and canonical tag, exactly as the live HTML carries them:
sections.code:
# /robots.txt — this journal's production site, as published
User-Agent: *
Allow: /
Disallow: /api/
Disallow: /admin/

Sitemap: https://ahmad-adbullah-prod.vercel.app/sitemap.xml

# The same site's article page — its own tags, from the live HTML
<meta name="robots" content="index, follow" />
<link rel="canonical"
      href="https://ahmad-adbullah-prod.vercel.app/blogs/shopify-core-web-vitals" />
sections.codeCaption: THE ACCESS LAYER, AS PUBLISHED — THIS JOURNAL'S ROBOTS.TXT AND AN ARTICLE PAGE'S OWN TAGS

sections.heading: Sitemap inclusion and internal links
paragraphs: With the access layer clean, the next stage is discovery: how does a crawler find the page in the first place? Two paths carry pages into a crawl — the sitemap, and the internal links from pages that are already crawled. Both are checkable against the output, not the intent.

The sitemap: the page's URL should appear in it, spelled exactly. A sitemap that omits the page, or lists it under the wrong host, is a discovery path with a hole in it. Submitting a sitemap does not guarantee crawling — Google's own [sitemap guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/sitemaps/build-sitemap) says that plainly — but a missing entry removes one of the two paths the page has. An excerpt of this journal's own live sitemap, real output, truncated:

The internal-link path is the one that gets overlooked: a page that is sitemapped but linked to from nowhere is a page the crawl may never reach through the site's own structure. Check that the page is reachable from the homepage in a handful of clicks, and that at least one indexed page links to it with the URL it should be indexed under. A page linked only from a filter state or a corner of the footer is a page the crawl finds, if it finds it at all.

<changefreq>monthly</changefreq>
<priority>1</priority>
</url>
<url>
