<!-- this journal's article URLs follow, one <url> per page -->
sections.codeCaption: THIS JOURNAL'S LIVE SITEMAP.XML — REAL OUTPUT, TRUNCATED

sections.heading: Duplicate, thin and low-value pages: the decision stage
paragraphs: A page can pass every access check and still not be indexed, because the index is a *quality decision*. The patterns that lose it: thin pages — a product page with a title and no substance, a collection with two products, a landing page that is a headline and a button; near-duplicates — ten URLs that are the same page with a query parameter; and low-value pages the store published for its own convenience rather than for a reader.

The [collection SEO notes from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-collection-seo) are the constructive version of this finding: a collection earns its standing when it is a real destination — a body of products, a useful description, a structure a shopper can navigate. A page that is eligible and still not indexed is not a bug to chase; it is a page the store should either grow into something worth indexing, or retire deliberately.

The structural version: a [migration](/blogs/shopify-migration-seo-checklist) that left half the old URLs dangling produces exactly this pattern at scale — a long tail of thin, duplicate, or unreachable pages that the index quietly declined, and a healthy core that nobody has connected to the declined half.

sections.heading: JavaScript rendering and content availability
paragraphs: One access check is specific to how modern stores are built. If the page's content — the title, the products, the text — renders by JavaScript after the initial load, the question is whether the crawler sees it. Shopify themes are server-rendered in the places that matter, which is most of why the platform is indexable at all; but a theme that moved its product content into client-side rendering, or an app that injects the page's substance after load, changes the answer.

The check is the same one a customer's browser runs: view the page's initial HTML — not the rendered screen — and ask whether the page's substance is in it. A page whose initial HTML is a shell and a script tag is a page that hopes the crawler runs the script and waits. It usually does — but the hop fails in the corners: the slow crawl, the partial render, the visit before the content was ready.

The fix, when the check fails, is to put the content in the HTML the server sends. For a store whose theme has drifted into client-side content, that is a theme change in the real sense — [development work](/shopify-development) with a verifiable outcome: the initial HTML of every important page, carrying the page's substance.

sections.heading: Requesting validation and monitoring the change
paragraphs: With the access and discovery layers clean, the tool offers *a validation* — a request asking Google to look at the page again. It does not command the index; it asks for a re-look, and it may end in the same answer if the page has not changed underneath.

The sequence is: fix what the checklist found, confirm the fix in the output (the status, the tags, the sitemap entry, the initial HTML), and only then request the validation. Requesting it against an uncorrected page is a ritual with no information in it; requesting it against a corrected page is the signal that the page is ready to be judged on *new evidence*.

The monitoring after is a habit, not a one-off: the URL Inspection state for the page in question, checked over the following weeks; the coverage report for the pattern, to see whether the finding was one page or a class of pages; and the crawl stats, which say whether the site is being visited at all in the quantities the store expects. The earning is visible in the data the owner's Search Console holds — the one instrument in this checklist that is the owner's to read.

sections.heading: What to do when a valid page is still not indexed
paragraphs: The last case is the one the checklists underprepare for: every check passes — 200, no noindex, self-canonical, sitemapped, linked, server-rendered, substantial — and the page is still not indexed. The answer has two parts.

The first is time. New URLs, and new stores, are indexed on a schedule that belongs to the index, not the store. A page that is eligible and recently published may simply be waiting — and the [product schema guide](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors) is the reference for making sure the page is at least readable while it waits. A page that presents a clean, consistent record is a page the index has no reason to distrust.

The second is the unflattering question: is the page worth indexing? The index declines pages it judges not useful, and the store that publishes a hundred thin variations of itself is a store whose pages are declined in bulk. The move is fewer, better pages — the page that deserves the URL, with the body of content a reader would come for — and retiring or merging the rest, which is the [journal's own discipline](/blogs) in miniature.

That is the checklist's ending: the store gets to make the page eligible, ask for the look, and improve the page the decision was about. The decision itself belongs to the index, and a store that understands the boundary spends its effort where it can actually move things — the access, the discovery, and the quality of the page that arrives.

takeaway: Indexing is a sequence of stages, and the page that is missing is missing at one of them. Check access, then discovery, then quality — in the output, not the settings — and the page that is still quiet is a page that has been asked, not a page that was ignored.

title: Shopify Google Merchant Center Errors: Product Feeds, Price Mismatches and Disapprovals
excerpt: A feed error is rarely about the feed: it is a disagreement between the record the channel reads and the page the customer lands on. The diagnostic loop that finds the source, corrects it, and verifies the fix held.
intro: Your product is available in Shopify, but the shopping channel reports an error — or shows a different price than the store does. The useful question is not how to dismiss the warning. It is which data source is inconsistent, and where it should be corrected. A feed error is rarely about the feed: it is a disagreement between the record the channel reads and the page the customer lands on. This guide is the loop — find the disagreement, correct the source, and verify the fix held.

sections.heading: How Shopify product feeds connect to Merchant Center
paragraphs: The connection is a chain with a specific shape. The store's product data — titles, variants, prices, availability, images — is what the feed is generated from. The feed is published to Merchant Center on a schedule. Merchant Center's systems read the feed, and they also read the landing pages the feed points at. And the product's structured data on the page is a third reading of the same record.

Three renderings of one truth, each generated at a different time by a different layer. That shape explains the whole problem class. A price changed in the admin after the last feed generation: the feed says one price, the page says another, and the channel flags the mismatch. A variant that went out of stock: the feed still offers it, the page shows it sold out, and the diagnosis is the same. In most of these cases the feed is the honest party — a snapshot, right when it was taken.

The reference point for what the record must agree with is Google's [structured data guidance for merchants](https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/7331077): the product data, the identifiers, and the structured data on the landing page need to correspond. On the Shopify side, [the Catalog documentation](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-shopify-catalog) is where the representation of the product data that channels consume is documented. The loop below works in the space between those two documents.

docRefs.title: Structured data requirements for Merchant Center (Google)
docRefs.note: Google's reference for what product data, identifiers and structured data must correspond to on the landing page — the standard the diagnostics are enforcing.

docRefs.title: Shopify Catalog
docRefs.note: Shopify's explanation of the catalog layer that feeds and channels read their product data from.

sections.heading: Common mismatch categories: price, availability, identifiers and variants
paragraphs: The mismatch categories are few, and they repeat. Price is the first: the feed's price and the page's price differ, usually because a sale, a discount, or a manual price change landed between the feed's last generation and the channel's check.

Availability is the second: the feed offers a product or variant the page shows as unavailable — or, the nastier direction, the page sells something the feed says is gone, which is how a customer ends up ordering what the channel believes cannot be bought.

Identifiers are the third: a GTIN, MPN, or brand that the feed reports differently from the page's structured data — a typo in one layer, a missing value in the other. The identifier mismatch is the quietest, because the page still looks perfect; the disagreement lives in the *machine-readable corners*.

Variants are the fourth, and the one that multiplies the problem: a product with twenty variants has twenty prices, twenty availability states, and twenty identifiers to keep in agreement, and one sold-out variant is one mismatch in a product that otherwise looks clean. A feed that reports the product as available because one variant is available — while the variant the customer selected is not — is technically correct and commercially wrong.

Each category has a telling habit: price mismatches cluster around sales cycles, availability mismatches around restocks, identifier mismatches around imports and bulk edits, variant mismatches around the combinations nobody orders. The pattern in the diagnostics is a clue about which event introduced the drift.

sections.heading: Compare Shopify product data with the live landing page
paragraphs: The comparison runs in *three columns*, per flagged product: what the admin says, what the feed says, what the page says. Start with the admin — the product record, the variant with its price and stock — because that is where the truth lives. Then the feed, for the same product and variant, with the generation timestamp if the tool shows it. Then the page: the rendered price, the availability state, and the structured data in the HTML, read the way the [product schema guide](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors) describes.

The public product page is the version of the record the customer actually sees, and the one the channel checks against. The desktop product view of a documented storefront, shown below, is the shape of what you are reading: title, price, availability, variants — the rendered record, in full.

When the three columns disagree, the wrong one is usually the one furthest from the admin — the feed, generated last and reading from a snapshot, or the page's structured data, emitted by a layer that drifted. The admin's record is the reference point the other two are measured against, which is why the next step corrects the source rather than the symptom.

sections.heading: Inspect structured data and feed diagnostics
paragraphs: The diagnostics screen is the owner's to read — the Merchant Center account is the owner's, and I do not access it on the owner's behalf — but the reading follows a fixed pattern. For each flagged item: note the product, the field, the two values in dispute, and the timestamp of the feed generation. The diagnostic tells you where to look; it does not tell you which side is right, because it cannot — it only sees the disagreement.

Then read the page's structured data for the same product against the feed's values. The shape of the comparison, with fictionalized values — the structure is the point, and it is the structure every diagnostic resolves to:
sections.code:
# Flagged item: price mismatch, one variant of a product
# (values fictionalized; the columns are the diagnostic's shape)

source            value        note
---               ---          ---
admin record      849.00 GBP   the truth: variant price, in stock
feed (last gen)   799.00 GBP   generated before the price change
page (rendered)   849.00 GBP   correct — reads the live record
page (structured) 799.00 GBP   stale — emitter holds the old price

# The disagreement is between the feed and the structured data.
# The admin and the page agree. The source of the drift is the
# structured-data emitter, not the price.
sections.codeCaption: THE THREE COLUMNS OF A MISMATCH — FICTITONIZED VALUES, REAL STRUCTURE

sections.heading: Correct the source of the mismatch
paragraphs: The correction follows the attribution. If the feed is stale, the fix is the generation: a new feed generation, and a check on the schedule — a feed that generates weekly in a store that changes prices daily is a mismatch factory with a calendar. If the structured data is stale, the fix is the emitter that produces it — a theme template, an app, a snippet — corrected at the layer that holds the old value.

If the admin record itself is wrong — the price in two places, the availability not matching the stock, the identifier missing — then the feed and the page were both faithful, and the fix is the data. That is the [product data management guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) in its purest form: the catalogue as the single record every channel reads, and the discipline of keeping it one record. Editing the feed's value by hand fixes the snapshot and leaves the camera broken.

The boundary around this step: I do not work in a store's Merchant Center account, and the corrections there — regenerating the feed, resubmitting the item, reading the diagnosis — are *the owner's actions*. What I do is the Shopify side of the line: the admin record, the theme's structured data, the app's configuration, the generation setup — everything the channel reads but does not own. It is a clean line, and it is the difference between a fix that is permanent and a resubmission that decays.

sections.heading: Retest after syncing changes
paragraphs: The retest is the step that separates a fix from a hope. After the source correction, the sequence is: the feed regenerates, the channel re-reads it, the diagnostic clears — and the page's structured data is read again to confirm it moved with the correction. A correction nobody re-reads is a correction the next price change will silently undo.

The retest has a timing problem worth naming: the generation and the re-read are scheduled, not instant. A correction made on Monday may not be visible in the diagnostics until the next generation and the next check. The expectation to set with the owner is the sequence, not the moment: source corrected, feed regenerated, diagnostic re-read, structured data re-verified — each step done, in order, with the evidence of the previous one in hand.

And the retest extends past the flagged item to its neighbours. A price change that landed late for one product usually landed late for the batch it was part of; a stale emitter that held one old price holds it for everything it emits. Re-testing the flagged product plus five from the same batch is what converts one cleared diagnostic into a class of cleared ones.

sections.heading: Build a repeatable product-feed monitoring process
paragraphs: The one-off fix solves today's mismatch; the process solves next month's. The process is small and specific: a scheduled comparison of the feed's values against the page's rendered values for a sample of products — price, availability, identifier — run after the events that move the data: sales cycles, restocks, bulk imports, theme deploys, app updates.

Those are the same events that drive the [schema QA checklist](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors), because they move the same record under two different readers. A store that runs both checklists on the same trigger is running one discipline with two witnesses: the page's own markup, and the channel's diagnostics.

The standing signal is the diagnostic's *trend, not its count*: a store whose mismatches appear after every sale and clear after every regeneration has a schedule problem, not a data problem. A store whose mismatches appear on random products with no event behind them has an emitter problem.

sections.heading: When the issue requires app or integration support
paragraphs: Some mismatches are not data problems — they are integration problems, and they show the same face: a feed that disagrees with the page. The signature is that the admin record, the page, and the feed all look individually reasonable and disagree pairwise, because one of the layers is not reading from the others: an app that syncs prices to the feed on its own schedule, an app that rewrites the structured data for its own feature, a custom integration that writes the feed from a cache nobody refreshes.

The attribution test is the same one from the [variants guide](/blogs/shopify-product-variant-issues): change one layer, re-read the dispute. Disable the app, regenerate the feed, re-read the diagnostic — if the disagreement follows the app out, the app is the source. These are the engagements where the fix is a configuration change, an app replacement, or an integration rebuilt against the live record rather than a snapshot — [development work](/shopify-development) with a before and after that the diagnostics themselves will show.

And the note for the owner reading the diagnostics: a disapproval banner is not a verdict on the store. It is a report on one field of one product at one moment. The stores that get through the feed problems are not the stores without mismatches — they are the stores with a loop: read the diagnostic, find the source, correct the source, retest, and let the next drift be found while it is still one product instead of a sale. That loop is what the [Commerce Journal](/blogs) keeps reporting on, because every store that sells through a channel is running it whether it knows or not.

takeaway: A feed error is three renderings of one record that stopped agreeing. Read the three columns — admin, feed, page — correct the layer that drifted, and retest until the evidence says the agreement held.

title: Shopify Product Data Management: How to Fix Inconsistent Titles, Attributes and Metafields
excerpt: When the catalogue has hundreds of products, small inconsistencies multiply: one product says "navy", another "dark blue", and a third has no colour at all. The cleanup workflow that turns that into a standard.
intro: When a catalogue has hundreds of products, small inconsistencies multiply: one product says “navy”, another says “dark blue”, and a third has no colour attribute at all. The filters, the search, the feeds, and the structured data all read the same record, and they all inherit the mess. This guide is the cleanup workflow: how the inconsistency shows up, how to standardize without disrupting live listings, and how to make the standard stick.

sections.heading: What poor product data looks like in a growing Shopify store
paragraphs: It shows up as the store's own surfaces disagreeing with each other. The filter offers five colours that are really two. The search for “navy” misses the product titled “Midnight Blue”. The feed reports a brand string the page spells differently. The structured data carries an availability the page does not show. None of these is a bug in any one system — they are the same data problem wearing four surfaces.

The growth pattern matters. The catalogue starts clean, because it is small and one person knows it. Then growth happens — a new supplier with its own naming, a seasonal import, a teammate who types the way she spells — and the consistency one person held by memory gets replaced by a record nobody fully reads.

The cost is distributed, which is why it is underdiagnosed: a little friction in the filter, a little noise in the search, a little staleness in the feed. No single symptom is worth a project, and the total is the discovery experience quietly degrading — the same failure the [collection filters guide](/blogs/shopify-collection-filters-guide) describes from the customer's side and the [Merchant Center guide](/blogs/shopify-google-merchant-center-errors) describes from the channel's side.

sections.heading: Standardize titles, descriptions, options and attributes
paragraphs: The standard starts with the title, because it is the first field every reader meets. A title template is a decision, not a constraint: the product name, its category, and one or two distinguishing facts, in a fixed order with a fixed vocabulary. The template is what makes a hundred products written by different people at different times read like one store.

The attributes get the same treatment, and the attribute vocabulary is the real deliverable. If the store sells in colours, the store has a list of colours — a *controlled set*, spelled one way, enforced by the field. “Navy” is in the list; “Navy Blue”, “Midnight”, and “navy” are not, and the field does not accept them. A rule the store enforces, rather than a rule someone must remember.

Options and variants follow the same discipline: the option names the dimension (Size, Colour), the values are the controlled set, and the combination is a real purchasable fact — the ground the [variants guide](/blogs/shopify-product-variant-issues) stands on. A catalogue with standardized options is one whose variants can be resolved, filtered, fed, and rendered without a guess at every step.
The shape of the standard, as a before-and-after of a standardized attribute set (fictionalized sample data — the pattern is the point):
sections.code:
# Sample: the same three products before and after the standard
# (values fictionalized — the pattern is the point)

# BEFORE — the catalogue as found
title:             "Amazing Stroller Deal!!"        colour: "Navy"
title:             "Midnight Travel System"         colour: "dark blue"
title:             "Travel System (New)"            colour: (blank)

# AFTER — the standard applied
title:             "Babymore Travel System, 3-in-1, with car seat"   colour: Navy
title:             "Jogger Travel System, 2-in-1"                    colour: Navy
title:             "Compact Travel System, 2-in-1"                   colour: Charcoal

# The controlled vocabulary: Navy, Charcoal, Olive, Sand — spelled once,
# enforced by the field, readable by every layer that reads the catalogue.
sections.codeCaption: BEFORE AND AFTER A STANDARDIZED ATTRIBUTE SET — FICTITONIZED SAMPLE DATA

sections.heading: When to use metafields and metaobjects
paragraphs: The platform's options and tags carry the first layer of the standard — the options the store sells by, and the labels it files by. The second layer is where the standard needs structure: the attributes that power filters, feeds, comparisons, and the newer discovery surfaces. That is the territory of metafields and metaobjects, and the decision is a type decision, not a preference.

A metafield is a single extra field on a product — a weight, a care instruction, a compatibility note. A metaobject is a structured object with its own fields and, where needed, a defined set of values — the catalogue's vocabulary made a data type. The rule: a value that is one of a known set belongs in a defined field that enforces the set; a measurement belongs in a field with a unit; a description nobody filters on belongs in a plain field.

The mistake to avoid is the metafield as a second free-text column — an extra field with no type and no vocabulary, which recreates the inconsistency problem one level up. The [high-variant product guidance](https://shopify.dev/docs/storefronts/themes/product-merchandising/variants/support-high-variant-products) points the same direction from the theme side: the structure of the data decides the structure of the page. And [Shopify's Catalog documentation](https://www.shopify.com/blog/what-is-shopify-catalog) is where the representation of that data, as channels and discovery surfaces read it, is described.

sections.heading: Establish rules for required product fields
paragraphs: The standard becomes a practice when it has a rule for what may not be missing. The required-fields list is short and specific: the title in the template's shape, the category, the primary attributes of the product's type (a stroller has weight and fold dimensions; a candle does not), the price, the availability, and the images that carry the product's real appearance.

The rule is enforced *at the door*, not in the audit. A product that cannot be published without its required fields is a catalogue that stays clean by construction — the same move the [product record notes from Prime Baby Gear](/blogs/prime-baby-gear-product-data) describe from the store's side: a record complete enough that the page has something true to render.

The cost is real, and it is a business decision: requiring the fold dimension on every product is right for a stroller store and nonsense for a candle store. The rule fits the catalogue's type, and it gets reviewed when the type grows — which is also when the [AI discovery guide](/blogs/shopify-ai-search-product-discovery) argues for tightening it, because the new readers of the record cannot ask the team what “midnight” means.

sections.heading: Audit existing products without disrupting live listings
paragraphs: The existing catalogue gets an audit before it gets the standard, because a standard applied blind to a live catalogue is a change with no baseline. The audit is a *read-only pass* over the catalogue — every product scored against the standard: title shape, attribute completeness, vocabulary conformance, variant consistency — with the findings written as patterns, the way the [discovery audit](/blogs/shopify-ai-search-product-discovery) writes its findings.

The patterns become the backfill plan — and a backfill at catalogue scale is exactly the kind of project scoped on the [development service](/shopify-development) page — , and the backfill runs so it does not touch what is selling. A live listing's price, availability, and images do not move during a data cleanup; the cleanup touches the fields the standard covers, in batches, with a verification pass after each. A product page before and after the batch, side by side: same price, same stock, same images, better record. The desktop product view of a documented storefront, shown below, is the shape of the page that must survive the cleanup unchanged in everything the customer sees.

The audit also finds the products the standard should not cover: the discontinued line being retired anyway, the test product, the duplicate that should be merged. The decisions it produces — keep, fix, merge, retire — are the catalogue's actual inventory, in the sense that matters.

sections.heading: Bulk updates, imports and data validation
paragraphs: The backfill at scale is a bulk operation, and a bulk operation has its own discipline. The source of truth for the update is a document — a spreadsheet or an import file — that is itself checked before it touches the catalogue: the rows against the standard, the vocabulary values against the controlled set, the product identifiers against the live catalogue. A bulk update built on a bad file is the inconsistency problem applied at scale, on a schedule.

The import runs in batches with a verification pass between them — a sample of the updated products read back from the live catalogue and checked against the file, the same read-back discipline the [feed retest](/blogs/shopify-google-merchant-center-errors) uses. Batch size is a risk decision: ten products is a test of the pipeline, a hundred is a run, a thousand is an event that deserves its own day and its own rollback plan.

The *rollback plan* is the part that gets skipped: the pre-update state of the changed fields, recorded, so a bad batch can be undone field by field instead of rediscovered product by product. A data change to the catalogue deserves the same ceremony as a theme deploy — which is what the [QA checklists](/resources/shopify-qa-checklist) exist for on anything customer-facing.

sections.heading: Connect product-data quality to search, filters and AI discovery
paragraphs: The standard is an input to every reader the store has. The filters read the attribute vocabulary — a standardized colour is a filter that works, and the [filters guide](/blogs/shopify-collection-filters-guide) makes the connection explicit, option by option. The search reads the titles and descriptions — a templated title is a search that finds the product by the name the customer uses. The feeds read the prices, availability, and identifiers — and the [Merchant Center loop](/blogs/shopify-google-merchant-center-errors) is short when the source record is clean, because there is less to drift.

The newer discovery surfaces read the structured record directly — the attributes, the variants, the availability, as data rather than as pixels. That is the direction the [AI search guide](/blogs/shopify-ai-search-product-discovery) points at: the readers of the catalogue are becoming machines that cannot ask the team what “midnight” means, and the answer has to be in the record.

The through-line of the journal is the same one: the store's surfaces are renderings of its record, and the quality of the rendering is bounded by the quality of the record. A store that standardizes its data is raising the ceiling on every surface at once.

sections.heading: A reusable catalogue-governance checklist
paragraphs: The governance pass runs on a schedule, in a fixed order, and it is short enough to actually run.

The vocabulary: are the controlled sets current — do the colours the store actually sells match the list the fields enforce? The sample: a random ten products, scored against the standard — title shape, attribute completeness, vocabulary conformance, variant consistency. The events: since the last pass, what moved the data — an import, a supplier change, a new product type, an app update? Each event is a chance for drift, and the pass checks the events' output, not just the sample.

The surfaces: one filter, one search, one feed diagnostic — the three readers, each checked against the same sample, so the record and its renderings are verified together. The decisions: the findings written as patterns with owners — the field to tighten, the batch to run, the product to merge or retire.

A store that runs the pass and files the findings has done half the work. A store that runs the pass and closes the findings is the one whose catalogue stays a document instead of becoming an archive — which is the whole of product data management: the standard, the cleanup, and the practice that keeps the two alive.

takeaway: Inconsistency is a catalogue's way of telling you it stopped being a document. Give it a standard, enforce it in the fields, backfill in verified batches, and run the governance pass while the catalogue is still small enough to love.

title: Shopify B2B Storefront Problems: Company Accounts, Catalogues, Pricing and Buyer Workflows
excerpt: A wholesale customer who has to shop like a first-time retail buyer every visit is buying from a storefront that was not built for how their business buys. What B2B changes, what depends on the plan, and how to test the buyer journey.
intro: A wholesale customer needs account-specific pricing, larger quantities, and a repeatable reorder process. If they have to shop like a first-time retail customer every visit, the storefront was not built for how their business buys. I write this one for the stores that sell to both audiences — retail and business — because the B2B side is where a storefront's assumptions get stress-tested. This guide maps what changes, what depends on the plan, and how to test the buyer journey the way a business buyer actually walks it.

sections.heading: What changes when a Shopify store serves business buyers?
paragraphs: The retail journey is built around a decision: one person, one purchase, one checkout. The business journey is built around a relationship: a company, a catalogue of standing orders, a set of people who buy on its behalf, and prices that are negotiated rather than displayed. Every layer of the storefront that assumes the retail journey has to be revisited when a business buyer arrives.

The changes cluster in four places. Identity: the buyer is a person inside a company, and the company carries the terms. Catalogue: the business may see a different set of products, or different prices for the same products, than the retail customer. Quantity: the units of purchase are cases and packs, not single items. Repetition: the purchase is a standing order that repeats, and the repeat is the point.

Shopify offers these capabilities as part of its B2B features — company profiles, company-specific pricing, the workflows around them — and the [B2B documentation](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/b2b) is the primary reference for what the platform provides. The plan boundary, stated up front: the features are tied to specific Shopify plans and configurations, and the [developer documentation](https://shopify.dev/docs) is where the implementation side is documented. A store evaluating B2B should start from the current plan documentation, not from an assumption that every feature is universal.

sections.heading: Company accounts and buyer permissions
paragraphs: The company account is the unit the B2B storefront is organized around: the company holds the terms — its pricing, its catalogue visibility, its payment terms — and the people inside it hold roles. A buyer places the order, an approver signs it off, an admin manages the company's record. *The permission model* is the difference between “a customer who buys a lot” and “a company that buys on terms”.

The permission design is a business decision with a technical shape, and the shape is worth getting deliberate about. Who can place orders, who can approve above a threshold, who can edit the company's addresses, who can see the order history — each is a rule the storefront enforces. The shape of a permission matrix, with fictionalized values — the matrix is the design, not a real company:

role        place orders  approve > 5k  edit addresses  view history

sections.heading: Customer-specific catalogues and pricing
paragraphs: The second cluster is what the company sees. A company-specific catalogue is the set of products the company can buy — a wholesale line the retail customer never sees, or a retail line the company does not. A company-specific price is the price the company's orders carry. Both are the same idea: the record of the product is not one price and one visibility. It is a price and a visibility per relationship.

That idea has a data consequence the [product data guide](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) covers from the catalogue side: the product record grows *a dimension*. A product that is one price for retail and another for the company is a product with two offers, and the theme, the cart, and the feeds all have to carry the dimension without mixing it up. The [variants guide](/blogs/shopify-product-variant-issues) makes the same point at the variant level — the unit of commerce is the specific thing the customer buys, and for a B2B store it carries the company's terms as well as its size and colour.

The warning: company-specific pricing is where the store's own records start disagreeing with each other. The price the company was quoted, the price in the catalogue, the price on the order — three numbers that have to agree, and a store that carries them in three places will one day bill the wrong one. Terms live in one place, or they do not live anywhere.

sections.heading: Quantity rules, bulk ordering and repeat purchases
paragraphs: The third cluster is *the unit of purchase*. A business buyer does not buy one; they buy a case, a pack, a standing quantity — and the storefront has to state the unit clearly. A minimum order quantity, a step quantity (sold in increments of six), a unit price that applies per item but is ordered per case: each is a rule the product record carries and the page renders.

The rule is what the [product data standard](/blogs/shopify-product-data-management) enforces, and it is where B2B product records diverge most from retail ones. A retail product is a price and a stock. A B2B product is a price, a stock, a unit, a minimum, and a step. The page that states the unit, the minimum, and the step before the order — not after, at checkout — is the page a business buyer trusts, because the terms are told to them where they can act on them.

And the repeat: the standing order is the feature that justifies the investment. A reorder is a workflow: the company's last order, or a saved list, offered as the starting point of the next one. A buyer who reorders in three steps instead of rebuilding the order from scratch is a buyer who stays — and the three steps are a design decision about how much the store remembers of the relationship.

sections.heading: How to separate B2B and retail journeys
paragraphs: The stores that sell to both audiences face the design question the single-audience stores never meet: how do the two journeys coexist without contaminating each other? The retail customer should not see the wholesale price, the case quantities, or the company account flows; the business buyer should not be funneled through the retail experience with a note that says “ask about trade pricing.”

The separation is a set of decisions at each layer. Identity: the company account is a distinct state, entered deliberately — a login that carries the company's terms, not a toggle that changes the price under the customer's cursor. Catalogue: the company's products are the company's catalogue, rendered from the company's record, not the retail catalogue with prices swapped. Journey: the B2B checkout carries the company's payment terms, its addresses, its approval step; the retail checkout carries none of them.

The cleanest implementation puts the separation in the data, not the theme: the company's terms are the company's record, and the theme renders whichever record the visitor carries. A theme that swaps prices with a flag is a theme that will one day show the wholesale price to the retail customer — and the flag is the bug. It is the same class of failure the [schema guide](/blogs/shopify-product-schema-errors) describes at the markup level: one surface, two records, the surface showing the wrong one.

sections.heading: Product, cart and checkout testing for business buyers
paragraphs: The test path runs the journey a business buyer actually runs, in the company's state, checking the terms at every step. The product page: the company's price, the unit of sale, the minimum and the step, the availability — all of them, for the company, not the retail customer. The cart: the quantities in the company's units, the totals at the company's prices, the minimum order enforced and explained when it is hit.

The checkout: the company's payment terms, its addresses, the approval step where the role requires it — and the order, placed, carrying the company's identifiers so the fulfilment side knows whose terms it is shipping under. The test is the journey, not the features: a feature that works in isolation and breaks in the journey — the approval step that loses the cart, the case quantity that becomes a single at checkout — does not work.

The test also runs for the roles, not just the buyer: the approver's view of the pending order, the admin's view of the company's record, the buyer who hits an address the admin has not set. Each role is a journey, and each journey is a test. The [QA discipline](/resources/shopify-qa-checklist) that applies to the retail store applies here with one addition: the company's state is the fixture, and the fixture has to be real — a test company with the test terms, or the test has not tested the B2B part at all.

sections.heading: Which requirements depend on Shopify plan or configuration?
paragraphs: The plan question comes before the design, because the design is bounded by what the plan provides. Shopify's B2B capabilities — company accounts, company-specific pricing, the quantity and net-term workflows — are offered as part of specific plans, and the [current plan documentation](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/b2b) is the reference for what is available where. A store planning a B2B storefront reads the plan documentation first, and treats every assumption the documentation does not confirm as an assumption to verify, not a fact to build on.

The configuration side is the store's own: which features are turned on, which roles are defined, which catalogues are maintained. The configuration is where the plan's capabilities become the store's behaviour, and it is where the [development work](/shopify-development) lives — the theme that renders the company's journey, the integrations that carry the company's terms into the order, the flows that keep the two audiences' records apart.

The frame for the owner: the plan tells you the ceiling, the configuration tells you the build, and the design is the space between. A B2B storefront is not a feature switched on; it is a second journey the store commits to running, with its own data, its own tests, and its own maintenance. That is the commercial side of this guide, and it is the side that shows up in the [Commerce Journal](/blogs) when a store's B2B journey is built well enough to have something specific to report.

sections.heading: A B2B storefront discovery checklist
paragraphs: The discovery pass runs before the build, in a fixed order, and it ends with the plan.

The buyer: who is the business buyer — the role, the company's size, the standing order's shape. The journey is designed around the buyer, and a buyer that is not described is a journey that is not designed. The terms: the pricing model, the quantity rules, the payment terms, the approval flow — written down as the data the store will carry, with the single source for each one named. The catalogue: the products the company sees, the products it does not, and the rule that keeps the two sets apart. The journey: the buyer's path from the company's login to the confirmed order, drawn as the steps the storefront must render.

The plan: the documentation read, the capabilities confirmed against the current plans, and the gap between the design and the plan written as *the decision list* — what the plan provides, what the configuration must build, what the store must accept.

A store that has run the pass builds the B2B storefront against a set of answers instead of a set of assumptions. One that has not is designing in the dark — which is how a second audience ends up with a first-audience storefront wearing a trade-pricing note.

takeaway: A B2B storefront is a second journey, not a price toggle: the company's terms are data, the roles are the permissions, the reorder is the workflow, and the plan's boundary is the first design input — read it before you draw a single screen.
